questions.explanation: Most candidates formed a suvat equation that took the upward start into account and chose C. Take up as positive: the stone ends 12 m below where it was thrown, so s = −12 m, a = −9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>, t = 3.4 s. From s = ut + ½at<sup>2</sup>, u = (−12 + ½ × 9.81 × 3.4<sup>2</sup>) / 3.4 = 13 m s<sup>−1</sup>. Many candidates treated the displacement and acceleration as being in opposite directions, which gives about 20 m s<sup>−1</sup>, D. A few treated it as constant velocity, 12 / 3.4 = 3.5 m s<sup>−1</sup>, A. Choose a positive direction and stick to it for s, u and a.

Most candidates chose B or C. Starting from rest, s = ½at<sup>2</sup>. A graph of s against t<sup>2</sup> is a straight line through the origin whose gradient is ½a, so the acceleration is twice the gradient: C. Many candidates did not account for the ½ and chose B. Whenever you plot a straight-line graph, write the equation in the form y = mx and read the gradient off it.

Relatively few candidates answered correctly. N and P are a Newton's third-law pair, so they are equal, and very few candidates chose B. Options A, C and D were chosen about equally, which suggests guessing. Those who thought the ball was in equilibrium were likely to choose A or C. The ball is momentarily stationary, but its velocity is changing from downwards to upwards, so it has a large upward acceleration at that instant. The resultant force is therefore upwards, and N must be larger than W: D. Stationary for an instant does not mean in equilibrium.

Many candidates correctly found the magnitude of the resultant momentum. Momentum is a vector and the paths are perpendicular: X has 4M × v = 4Mv and Y has M × 3v = 3Mv, so the magnitude is √((4Mv)<sup>2</sup> + (3Mv)<sup>2</sup>) = 5Mv, C. A 3-4-5 triangle shows up here. Many chose D, 7Mv, which adds the two magnitudes. Few chose A (taking the difference) or the option that treated the objects as equal in mass.

Many candidates correctly chose C. An object floats in equilibrium when the upthrust equals the weight of water displaced, and the hydrostatic pressure is not the same at all points on the object, because it increases with depth: the pressure on the underside is larger than on the top, and that difference produces the upthrust. B and D were chosen by those who did not realise that the pressure on a point of the object increases with depth. A confuses the upthrust depending on the volume of water displaced with the upthrust being equal to a volume. Two different types of quantity cannot be equal to one another: a force cannot equal a volume.

Most candidates correctly saw that the change in energy is just mgh. The object rises at constant speed, so its kinetic energy does not change in time t, and the energy gained is gravitational potential energy: mgh, A. Many candidates chose B, not realising the kinetic energy does not change. A few chose C, mgv, which is a rate of change of energy, a power, rather than an energy. Check the unit: the question asked for an energy, so joules, not watts.

A majority of candidates correctly related kinetic energy to time. Falling from rest with no air resistance, v = gt, so E<sub>K</sub> = ½mv<sup>2</sup> = ½mg<sup>2</sup>t<sup>2</sup>: a curve that gets steeper, C. Very few chose D, so most realised the kinetic energy increases as the object falls. A is the graph of velocity against time, mistaken for kinetic energy, or candidates who forgot that kinetic energy is proportional to the velocity squared. B has the shape of an object approaching terminal velocity, which would need significant air resistance, and the question says it is negligible.

Most candidates correctly chose A. The wire obeys Hooke's law, so the energy stored is E = ½Fe = ½ke<sup>2</sup>, and the extension is proportional to √E. Plotting the extension (y) against the energy (x) gives a curve that bends over towards the x-axis, as in the graph: A. Many candidates chose D, recognising that the curved graph must relate the extension and the elastic potential energy, but swapping the axes: energy against extension curves upwards. A few chose B or C, which would be straight lines for a wire that obeys Hooke's law, since force and extension are proportional.

Candidates were reminded to read the conditions carefully: the intensity of the transmitted light is zero at the start, so the graph must start at zero. Many recalled that the intensity varies as cos<sup>2</sup>θ and so goes through two cycles in 360°, and most of the candidates chose A or B. B starts at I<sub>0</sub>, not at zero, so it is ruled out by the starting condition. Some thought the intensity varies as cosθ, which gives a single cycle, and chose C or D. A starts at zero, rises to I<sub>0</sub> at 90°, and does so twice in 360°: A.

Many candidates correctly chose A: transverse waves can diffract, as can any wave. The wrong answers were chosen about equally, so those who did not know that transverse waves can diffract were guessing. B is false because only stationary waves have nodes and antinodes. Sound in air is longitudinal, so C is false. Transverse waves can be formed on a spring, so D is false too.

Some candidates correctly recalled that the vertical distance from a peak to a trough is twice the amplitude. In time t the object goes peak to trough, then back to the peak, so it moves 2a + 2a = 4 times the amplitude: D. Many chose C, confusing the amplitude with the peak-to-trough distance: twice the amplitude is only half of the journey. Some chose A, confusing the distance a wavefront travels horizontally with the vertical distance the object moves.

Many candidates correctly found the fringe separation: from the first to the tenth bright fringe there are 9 spacings, so x = 22 / 9 = 2.4 mm. The double-slit equation then gives a = λD / x = (500 × 10<sup>−9</sup> × 3.5) / (2.4 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) = 0.72 mm: C. Many thought the separation was 22 / 10 = 2.2 mm, which gives 0.80 mm, D. Many treated the whole 22 mm as the fringe separation, which gives 0.080 mm, A. Count the gaps, not the fringes.

Most candidates treated the wave as a progressive wave and chose B, but this is a stationary wave. All the points between two adjacent nodes move in phase, and points in adjacent loops are in antiphase. The diagram shows two loops: R and S in the upper loop and T and V in the lower. V is moving down, so T, in the same loop, is also moving down. R and S are in the other loop, so both move up: D. Some candidates did realise this. A and C were also chosen by many, with C slightly more popular, but neither corresponds to a possible motion of the wave.

Candidates had to consider the next two waves that can be set up in a tube closed at one end: a node at the mouthpiece and an antinode at the bell. The frequencies are odd multiples of the fundamental: 75 Hz, then 3 × 75 = 225 Hz, then 5 × 75 = 375 Hz: D. Many candidates correctly found this. Those who took the next higher frequencies as integer multiples chose B (150 and 225 Hz). Those who thought the frequency would double each time chose C (150 and 300 Hz). Those who took 1.5 and 2 times the fundamental chose A (113 and 150 Hz).

A majority of candidates chose A or B, possibly recalling sketches of how the resistance of an LDR varies with light intensity. The question asks for the variable resistor, though. The LDR's resistance falls as the intensity rises, and for the total to stay the same, R must rise by the same amount: R = constant − R<sub>LDR</sub>, a curve that rises and levels off: A. Many also chose B, either confusing the behaviour of the LDR or misreading the question and giving the LDR's own graph. Very few chose D: the LDR's resistance does change, so R has to change as well.

Very few candidates chose B, perhaps because a circuit with zero current is unfamiliar. With no current there is no p.d. across the internal resistance, so the terminal p.d. equals the e.m.f. Many chose A, without realising that the statement equates a potential difference, which is energy per unit charge, with a total energy. Many chose C, confusing the e.m.f. with the terminal p.d. and also not noticing that the statement describes a quantity of energy, not a ratio of energy to charge. Read every option carefully, units and all.
